items.title: Apple's iOS 28 schedule shift helps engineers get more creative
items.content_html:
Apple has experimented with how it develops its operating system updates, with early schedule changes in making the 28-gen updates, letting engineers become more creative earlier in the process.

Like any major project, Apple's annual operating system updates like iOS 27 require some intense scheduling. However, the way you schedule work can have a big impact on the final result.

According to Mark Gurman in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg on Sunday, Apple has made a tweak to how it works on its operating system updates.

For iOS 28 and iPadOS 28, known internally as Bell, as well as macOS 28, known as Poppy, the earliest stage of development was adjusted.

Apple has three major milestones for its operating systems, named M1, M2, and M3, throughout the annual cycle. The change occurred to M1, which has already passed.

Normally, each stage lasts for eight weeks, starting with four weeks of coding and then four weeks of convergence. The convergence refers to integrating the newly developed features into the operating systems.

However, this time around, Apple has shifted the split in favor of more coding in M1. That is, six weeks of coding and feature development followed by just two weeks of convergence.

A favorable shift

Employees apparently like this change, in part because it enables creativity. The engineers get more time to come up with ideas and to work through them, before having to lock them down and work them into the operating system.

This view certainly makes sense, especially if you consider the entire development cycle. As the year goes on, there will be a greater focus on correctly integrating the features into the operating system than earlier in the year.

Later stages will have previously added features from earlier stages to manage, as well as those incorporated in the milestone period. Earlier stages do not have this to worry about, so the convergence period isn't as important.

By shifting the schedule slightly, those early M1-stage features get more time to be worked on before convergence. The hope is that the extra time to come up with features will improve their overall quality too.

items.title: Siri AI won't get more control of Apple apps until Spring 2027
items.content_html:
Siri is already capable of handling some tasks for iOS 27.3 developer beta users. Apple is exploring making it even more useful to keep up with rival AI apps.

Developers in iOS 27.3 are discovering that Siri AI can do a lot more for users. For first-party apps, users can ask Siri what it can do, and then ask for it to carry out those same tasks.

However, this is only one step for Apple. It wants to do a lot more, both in terms of task complexity and for third-party apps too.

In Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman points out this Siri AI capability, but adds that this extended support for Apple's own apps can arrive to the public version in December.

Third-party support is still on the way, but that won't happen until the spring of 2027 as part of a "preview." This will probably be part of iOS 27.5 or iOS 27.6, ahead of the 2027 WWDC.

A more productive future

The moves, which Apple has planned as App Intents for quite some time, are important but behind other AI apps in terms of sophistication.

Services like Muse and Grok are capable of handling tasks and working between conversations. They can also elect to pause and resume work on their own, depending on the project's needs and the user's preferences over time.

Apple is allegedly trying to move in that direction, in terms of providing long-term assistance to users for specific tasks without necessarily needing user oversight every step of the way.

This more agentic style of Siri could also arrive early in 2027.

items.title: Apple leadership may have differing views on AI strategy
items.content_html:
A new report suggests Apple still faces internal battles around AI strategy even though it has seemingly held to the same strategy set by John Giannandrea nearly a decade prior.

The usual chatter and rumors that make it out of containment to reporters' ears suggest catastrophe and confusion within Apple even as evidence suggests otherwise. In a world where the AI bubble is bursting, if not at least deflating faster by the day, it's odd to see reports continue to suggest Apple has a poor strategy.

According to the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg, CEO John Ternus has asked Craig Federighi to produce more AI faster, even as the report contradicts itself and suggests Federighi's planning is already on too short of a timeframe. The report doesn't reflect the realities as they have been observed externally, where Apple has kept a cool head and avoided billions in losses and wasted investment versus its competitors.

There is no doubt some such meeting took place between Apple's software chief and CEO, but the tone of that meeting was likely very different. Those willing to share rumors based on "knowledge of the matter" likely have an axe to grind.

Then there's the added color and need for some kind of negative narrative from that publication. So, needless to say, this particular story can be taken with a grain of salt, just like with rumors of Srouji's departure.

The report goes on about other leadership position shifts and potential departures, but like we've learned, it's best not to dwell on such internal gossip and speculation until something happens.

Apple's AI strategy is well known

Apple hired John Giannandrea from Google in an effort to push its AI and ML strategy forward in 2018. His strategy focused on building powerful hardware that could handle smaller local models instead of chasing a trillion-dollar frontier model that required miles of data centers and GPUs.

In spite of suggestions otherwise, Apple has stuck to that strategy throughout. Investors did demand to see Apple's efforts in 2024, which led to an over-ambitious WWDC that promised more than Apple could deliver at the time.

A reset in approach, a rebuild of Siri, and a relaunch in 2026 with Google's Gemini frontier model at its core allowed Apple to maintain its focus in spite of mounting pressures. Today, Apple's hardware is among the best built for local AI processing. Its Apple Foundation Models serve good-enough private and secure functions useful for its user base.

Meanwhile, tech stocks drop as political pressure increases and the artificial demand represented by unfinished data centers is challenged by potential regulation. Apple remains unaffected by such moves and benefits from its private, secure, and local-first approach.

items.title: Siri AI chief may step down as more Apple departures are rumored
items.content_html:
Apple's Mike Rockwell is reportedly considering leaving at least his current role as head of Siri AI, perhaps prompting a shakeup of executive roles at the company.

Rockwell was behind the development of the Apple Vision Pro and subsequently became head of Siri AI as Apple worked to revamp Siri into the version released in 2026. According to Bloomberg's "Power On" newsletter, though, he is seriously contemplating his future.

Reportedly, this could comprise his stepping down as lead of Siri AI during 2027. However, it might further mean his leaving Apple altogether.

The new report has no further detail, but speculates that if Rockwell makes either move, his current responsibilities would probably be shared between two people. Those are ex-Google AI veteran Amar Subramanya, and Sebastien Marineau.

At present, Marineau reports to Craig Federighi and reportedly there is some expectation that he will eventually replace his boss. Although as the report also notes, there is presently no indication of Federighi planning to either retire or leave Apple in the short term.

How Rockwell reorganized Siri A

Mike Rockwell only took over Siri AI in March 2025, following Apple "fixer" Kim Vorrath's assessment of that team. By April, Rockwell was replacing staffers with people from his Apple Vision Pro work.

This all led to the release of the much-revamped and much improved Siri AI, which was announced at WWDC 2026. But the change in leadership from John Giannandrea to Rockwell reportedly came after crisis talks.

items.title: How Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph learns about your life on Mac
items.content_html:
A breakdown of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph shows what your Mac and Apple Intelligence know about you and your life.

The upgrade to Siri AI added the understanding of personal context to Apple Intelligence. By pulling information from messages, emails, and photos, Siri can come up with answers to queries with contextual elements, such as knowing the name of your mother from a travel itinerary.

However, Apple has been compiling data on its users for a lot longer, with macOS 13 doing so since 2022. In a breakdown by security researchers at Eighth Rank, the generation of a Personal Knowledge Graph in macOS is detailed, including the kinds of data it compiles and retains on your Mac.

A pair of daemons

The process starts with a pair of daemons that Apple includes in macOS, used to compile the knowledge graph. However, Apple doesn't offer much information about them, aside from the name "knowledgeconstructiond" and a brief explanation that it analyzes device content and creates a knowledge graph.

The daemons store work in the Library/IntelligencePlatform directory, which contains 51 SQLite databases. While stored in plaintext, they are kept in an area protected by TCC Full Disk Access.

One the researchers found interesting was graph.db, using 181 entity classes and 278 predicates, with each row consisting of a subject, an object, and a predicate.

The subject is an entity of some form, such as a person or an app, with objects being a plain value like a name or a date. The predicate says the kind of relationship the database believes there are between the subject and the object.

A Personal Knowledge Graph visualization - Image Credit: Eighth Rank

The list of entities ranges from things like "person," "group of humans" and "organism" to topics such as "person in the arts," "sports organization," and "political party." Predicates include "what kind of thing this is," "genre," "has religion," "topics a person is interested in," and the "face cluster for a person."

The bulk of the work of the daemons is to populate the database with these relationships over time. Other databases include a communication log that pulls information on your location and movement, and a long list of device signals.

There's also a stream titled ContextualUnderstanding.PhysicalSocial, which appears to be a list of people and contact details that the user would've been physically near at some point. However, the researchers didn't see this filled in at all.

Families and deletion

The daemons would plainly copy data points from sources, and makes rulings based on what it finds. This includes inferring if a new data point is related to existing points, such as if a name is for someone already listed in the knowledge graph.

This can use a lot of different elements to produce a ruling. To determine who is family to the user, models apparently looked at 144 mostly behavioral features, as well as analysis from Photos of people who appear in pictures with you.

Each row is given a confidence score between 0 and 1.

Other models and systems are just as complex, bt there's also a bit of complexity to the way it handles deleted data.

Deleting some reference, such as a contact, doesn't immediately delete it from the database. The main live graph is capable of forgetting, with deleted contacts simply disappearing as they don't get derived again by the system for maintenance.

A second table, "expired_stable_graph," is kept at the same time as the live graph. It contains retracted rows, complete with confidence and relationship scores, with data seemingly pruned from it after 48 hours.

The result is that a conclusion derived from the models can still outlive the information on the device that helped produce it.

Detailed, but locally stored

The breakdown indicates that there's a massive trove of data stored on a Mac, and in surprising detail. In its research, it could determine there was a child in the household and its age, the daycare it went to, and associated phone numbers.

It was also capable of determining where a family would be, at what time, and for how long, as well as who would be at that place at that time.

From a privacy standpoint, it may seem concerning to have this amount of information and at such a granular level, all to drive things like Siri's personal context capabilities.

But at the same time, bear in mind this is locally-stored data on a Mac being analyzed here. It's a lot more private than what other AI-centric firms are producing in the cloud, because that data does end up leaving your device.

items.title: Claude gets AirPods 3 head tracking working on Linux
items.content_html:
AI has been used to find out how to access motion tracking data from AirPods, enabling one Linux user to use head tracking data to produce a software mouse.

AirPods and AirPods Pro have head tracking capabilities thanks to some built-in motion-detecting sensors. While it is currently used for things like Spatial Audio and Siri Interactions, one enterprising user has taken steps to widen their use on Linux.

Apple does allow AirPods and other earphones to work on Linux and other platforms by functioning as standard Bluetooth headphones. They can be used for normal listening, but things like head tracking are not available once you leave Apple's ecosystem.

In a Reddit post on Friday, Matteo Guaduisi said they wanted to control their mouse using a pair of AirPods 3 on Linux. However, they said that every open source project in the same field said that AirPods 3 were not supported.

AI as hardware hacker

Driven by this apparent lack of support, they spent an afternoon using Claude Code to find out how AirPods 3 work when it comes to motion tracking.

At one point, AI agents were instructed to check other similar projects in the background for an answer. This turned out to be a good idea, as one agent uncovered the answer in iOS framework code.

It turned out that AirPods 3 uses a different protocol than the Pro models.

The data also wasn't being sent over due to the use of a restrictive default setting. The default Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) was too small for both the standard audio data and motion sensor data, so the latter was excluded.

After fixing that, the head tracking data was streaming over Bluetooth at 200hz.

The effort eventually led to the creation of the MousePods project, which reads the motion sensor data of AirPods 3 and AirPods Pro in Linux. As the name implies, a user's head movements translate into pointer movements on the desktop.

Crucially for AirPods users, the project relies on changes on the Linux host end, not anything directly affecting the AirPods firmware. If you do experiment with this, you're not going to be left with non-functional AirPods, or anything that breaks a warranty.

The project has also released the code as "Open" and for others to use in their own projects.

Software but no broken AirPods

The project is an interesting one, as it shows how AI is evolving in its use. We had the initial phase of AI being not exactly a smart entity then becoming somewhat better, and then the start of the vibe coding era.

As the idea of using AI to handle tough coding tasks has taken hold, the attention has turned to affecting existing software. While games had mods that did the same thing in a relatively non-destructive manner, it's now being used to tackle code in a more direct fashion.

Not just people making Adobe product recreations or hackers attacking systems. There are some who are using AI to make new firmware for devices, like cameras, changing how they function completely.

To be clear, you really should check your device's warranty before going down this route. Depending on what the warranty states, it may not be acceptable to change the software of a device beyond any official firmware updates.

If it breaks when you mess with it, that's your money down the drain.

One unusual application of AirPods surfaced in July, after one developer turned them into a Frisbee stat tracker. After attaching an AirPod to a flying disc, motion data can be sent to the Kinapod Disc app running on an iPhone, including spin rate, total revolutions, and estimated release speed.

While in that case it was an application on Apple hardware, the Kinapod Disc app also preserved the utility of the AirPods without changing any firmware.

That said, the MousePods project is handled in a way that doesn't require any firmware update at all. It is a very non-destructive method of solving the problem, and gives other developers a glimpse into how the technology works.

Even on platforms outside of Apple's ecosystem.

items.title: New Apple Music Classical update matches wider Music rebrand
items.content_html:
Apple has continued its Apple Music rebrand, bringing a new black-and-white icon and revamped user interface to its Apple Music Classical app for iPhone and iPad.

The new update follows a larger rebrand that has removed the familiar red coloring from Apple Music's icon and marketing materials. It also used the new design identity when unveiling Apple Music Hall in Battersea, London.

Alongside the removal of red as a base color, the new look includes blue accents throughout. This even extends to the use of blue links rather than the traditional red ones that users are more accustomed to.

Notably, Apple's release notes do not mention the new look. Instead, they simply point to improvements to the app's stability and performance.

Apple Music Classical looks great on iPhone Duo

Apple Music Classical streams music in much the same way as the standard Music app, but with adjustments made to better accommodate classical works. Classical music doesn't always fit into the traditional album-based framework of most music apps, something the Apple Music Classical app counters with a bespoke design.

Apple Music Classical plays host to a wide array of music

The newly updated app builds on the previous Liquid Glass update that arrived alongside iOS 26 in 2025. It now more closely matches the rest of Apple's first-party offerings, especially Apple Music.

The newly updated app is available for download from the App Store now. Apple Music Classical is included as part of the Apple Music subscription at no extra cost, and has its own apps across Apple's platforms.

items.title: Swipeblocked catalogs the phrases Apple's keyboard won't suggest
items.content_html:
Your iPhone's reluctance to suggest certain words runs the gamut from bodily functions all the way to Santa Claus, revealing some interesting boundaries in Apple's keyboard dictionary.

A new website, Swipeblocked, wants you to know that there are thousands of words and phrases your iPhone will not let you say. Except it will let you say every single one of them.

It just won't put those words in your mouth. Or hands, I suppose.

"The iPhone keyboard carries a hidden list of thousands of phrases it will never suggest or let you swipe," the website reads. "Alongside slurs, sex and drugs, the list covers political slogans, historical events and public figures."

To be clear: this isn't a new feature. For a long time, Apple has prioritized certain autocorrects and swiped words over others.

There is a reason for this. For example: a few slurs are one letter off from words you're more likely to use.

If Apple were to suggest those words instead of the more plausible word, it would land itself in hot water. Not to mention, no one wants to have to explain "I didn't mean to send that."

Unsurprisingly, autocorrect, predictive text, and swipe won't suggest offensive words. And how does it suss out what is and isn't offensive?

A massive internal dictionary, of course.

Apple's internal dictionary actually has three categories for words it won't suggest: vulgar, offensive, and sensitive. The full list of the offending words, along with what category they fall under, is here.

Of course, it's a good time to remind you that these words are, in fact, offensive. So if you click the link, you at least should know what you're in for.

Apple isn't stopping you from typing the whole word out yourself

As Swipeblocked points out: nothing stops you from typing any of these words. Apple just won't go out of its way to suggest them.

There are, however, other words and phrases that Apple's keyboard doesn't suggest, even if they don't fall in the aforementioned list. "Left wing conspiracy" is the one Swipeblocked mentions, saying that it changes it to "left wrong conspiracy."

Of course, halfway down the page it also points out that you can't swipe or predict "right wing conspiracy" or left and right wing propaganda.

Amusingly enough, you can't say "Santa isn't real" via swipe or predictive text, either.

"Apple doesn't publish the list or say how it's chosen. This site decodes it from the keyboard's own data files, as of iOS 27," Swipeblocked notes.

If you'd like to see the entire list of English blocked words and phrases, you can check them out here. Many of them are complete gibberish, such as "am some number ones most corrupt," so I'm not entirely sure what this list proves in the long run.

And, as Swipeblocked mentions, English isn't the only language that has suggestion blocks, either. It's every language, and for cultural reasons, some languages have different blocks than others. Don't salute the World War II German dictator, for instance.

At any rate, we here at AppleInsider are treating this as a curiosity. It's interesting to pull back the curtain from time to time to see how the technology works, but it shouldn't be seen as Apple's attempt to control how its users speak to each other.

items.title: Developers have optimized over 100,000 apps for the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
Apple says that developers have been rapidly adapting their apps for the iPhone Duo's twin screens, with thousands of new ones being added daily.

The lack of apps that hadn't been updated for the iPhone Duo was definitely the device's Achilles' heel. But as AppleInsider said, that problem was small, getting smaller, and by the time most buyers get their iPhone Duo, it will be gone.

Now in a statement to AppleInsider, Apple has boasted about the rate at which developers are updating to take advantage of the iPhone Duo.

"It's been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we're grateful for their creativity and innovation," Susan Prescott, Apple's vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations. "Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day."

Prescott made similar remarks in late October 2026, but since then has added more detail about how Apple is working with developers.

"In the last month alone, thousands of developers have joined us for workshops in 19 cities around the world to experience iPhone Duo firsthand and bring updated apps to their users," she said. "The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we're excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo."

Separately, a particularly notable update for the iPhone Duo has been from Google. Larger firms such as Google and Microsoft have often been very late to adopting new Apple requirements, but Google has rapidly updated its Maps app.

Why apps need updating

If developers have consistently followed Apple's recommendations, then their apps already make some use of the iPhone Duo's two screens. But to fully use the width of both the external and internal screens, developers need to do some work.

How the updated Google Maps uses the whole of the inner and outer displays on the iPhone Duo.

Apple says that this extra work is minor. But if developers have not been following those recommendations, then the effort needed is much more substantial.

It's also much more important, too. Such apps are shown in the center of the inner screen with large black bars to left and right.

Users can expand the app to more or less fill the screen, but it looks poor. Plus users can drag such an app to one side of the screen or the other, and then open a second app to fill up the rest of the screen.

But then beyond their appearance, apps that have been properly updated for the iPhone Duo make extra use of the device's form factor. Apps can tell how wide open the device is, for instance, and adjust their controls to best serve the user.

items.title: iPhone 20 range rumored to ditch Action Button
items.content_html:
The Action Button may soon be dropped, but if you thought that would mean getting back the much-missed mute switch, think again.

Back in 2023, the Action Button began replacing the mute switch on ever iPhones, but that stopped with the launch of the iPhone Duo. Now prolific leaker Instant Digital claims that it's about to be history.

Writing on the Chinese social media site Weibo, they say (in translation) that "Apple's Action button... will officially be phased out starting with new iPhone models in the second half of next year." So presuming Apple sticks to its new split iPhone launch, that may mean that the 20th anniversary iPhone will be the first to lose it.

"It will be integrated with the camera button," the leaker continues. "Tap to launch the camera, press and hold... to perform [the Action Button's] function."

The camera button referred to is presumably the iPhone's Camera Control. This already launches the camera with one tap, but pressing longer is already a way to use Visual Intelligence.

If correct, the Action Button would be the first iPhone control to be removed since that button replaced the mute switch.

While it's unusual for Apple to do this, the company must know how much or how little it is used. Whatever the figures are, they weren't high enough to make finding space for the Action Button on the iPhone Duo a priority.

Then there is also that the button and what its settings are hasn't been significantly updated since launch. There is still the peculiar design that pressing it once does nothing but display a notice telling you to press longer.

Nonetheless, pressing and holding has proved a quick enough way to launch one action or, via Shortcuts, multiple ones. But, speaking of Shortcuts, it is already possible to emulate practically every benefit of the Action Button with a lock screen icon.

The Action Button was first introduced on the Apple Watch Ultra.

Note that Weibo leakers do not have a great track record. Instant Digital has sometimes posted what seems more like wishful thinking than an actual leak.

Even so, removing the Action Button does seem plausible given its absence on the iPhone Duo.

Apple had hopes for the Action Button

The Action Button first appeared on the Apple Watch Ultra back in September 2022. Then it came to the iPhone with the iPhone 15 Pro the following year and the smart money would've bet on it coming to the iPad eventually.

It never did, but Apple certainly had more plans for the Action Button, at least at one stage.

In 2024, for instance, a patent revealed that there could even be more than one Action Button, albeit on iPhone cases instead of the device itself.

items.title: Apple Store holiday return rules are in effect
items.content_html:
As it always does, in the run up to the holidays Apple has extended its return window. With some exceptions, buyers now have until early January 2027 to change their minds.

Apple does this every year, and each time the broad strokes are the same. From now until Christmas Day, most items can be returned until a date in early January.

For this year, Apple has announced that the return date is January 8, 2027. It has also, though, detailed what is excluded from that:

  • Apple Gift Cards
  • Apple developer membership and other products
  • Installed software or upgrades from the App Store

Most importantly, though, is what happens with the return of an iPhone or a cellular iPad, if it were bought locked to a particular carrier.

"Wireless carriers have different service-cancellation policies," notes Apple. "Returning your iPhone or iPad may not automatically cancel or reset your wireless account."

Consequently Apple says that you "are responsible for your wireless service agreement."

Note, too, that Apple's returns policy only applies to items bought from either a retail Apple Store or its online one. In the case of an online order, the date the product is received is used to determine eligibility, not the order day.

All of this is the same as before, except that Apple has added back in its rejection of gift cards which it omitted in 2025. For completeness, the terms and conditions still include references to opened software, decades since Apple sold any apps in boxes.

These are the terms as apply to US customers, although there are very similar ones for international buyers. There is also a series of additional returns steps for customers in Puerto Rico, which Apple details on its returns page.

items.title: HomePod mini 2 review - Six years later, not enough reasons to upgrade yet
items.content_html:
The $149 HomePod mini 2 sounds slightly better and offers expanded connectivity, but neither improvement gives existing owners a compelling reason to upgrade.

Six years after the original HomePod mini arrived, Apple's second-generation speaker brings more than a faster processor. New Mac audio capabilities, four-speaker surround sound for Apple TV 4K, and upgraded wireless hardware expand what the compact speaker can do beyond playing music.

The HomePod mini 2 launched on October 30, 2026, without Siri AI, one of its most anticipated features. Until Apple delivers that update, the newer model makes a stronger case for first-time buyers and people expanding their setups than for anyone replacing a perfectly good original.

Sound GlowSupported with software 27.2Supported
Smart homeApple Home hub, Thread, temperature and humidity sensorsApple Home hub, Thread, temperature and humidity sensors
Ultra WidebandYesYes
Dimensions3.3 x 3.9 inches3.3 x 3.9 inches
Weight0.76 pound0.74 pound
ColorsWhite, blue, orange, yellow, midnightWhite, blue, pink, green, midnight

The spec upgrades look great in a vacuum. It all comes down to how it works together, though, to deliver music.

Better sound, but not a dramatic improvement

The HomePod mini 2 delivered clear, balanced sound throughout our testing, with excellent room coverage and plenty of volume for everyday listening. Our initial comparison with the original HomePod mini didn't reveal much difference.

A second round of testing with lossless music brought out a modest improvement.

We listened to classical, metal, and dubstep to hear how the device handled different instruments, arrangements, and musical styles. With lossless playback enabled, the HomePod mini 2 offered slightly better instrument separation, making individual sounds easier to distinguish.

The improvement was noticeable when we listened closely, although it wasn't dramatic enough to change the overall experience. The original HomePod mini still sounds remarkably good for its size, and the newer model doesn't leave its predecessor behind.

The HomePod mini 2 also maintained consistent sound quality across the locations we tested. We could move the speaker between shelves, tables, and other convenient spots without losing the clarity or room coverage we enjoyed.

Apple continues to use a full-range driver and two passive radiators, with computational audio adjusting playback in real time. The newer S10 processor has considerably more processing power than the original S5, although both generations retain the same general speaker configuration.

The HomePod mini 2's improved instrument separation gives it a small but welcome advantage, particularly for listeners who pay attention to the finer details of their music. For everyone else, the original still delivers much of the same listening experience without requiring another purchase.

Familiar design with a faster processor

Anyone familiar with the original HomePod mini will recognize the second-generation model immediately. Apple has kept the rounded, mesh-covered design and illuminated touch surface, with controls for playback and volume on top.

The HomePod mini 2 measures 3.3 inches tall and 3.9 inches wide, making it easy to fit on a desk, shelf, or bedside table. Apple has refreshed the color selection with pink and green, replacing the original generation's orange and yellow options alongside blue, white, and midnight.

Inside, the S10 replaces the original S5 processor, while Wi-Fi improves from Wi-Fi 4 to Wi-Fi 6E. Bluetooth also moves from version 5.0 to Bluetooth 6, with Thread networking and Ultra Wideband support carrying over from the original.

The faster processor brings more potential benefits than just audio processing. Separate hands-on testing found that Siri responded more quickly and Handoff transferred audio faster than on the original HomePod mini.

There's also an important limitation for anyone planning to mix old and new HomePods. Apple requires two speakers of the same model and generation for stereo pairing, so an original HomePod mini can't form a stereo pair with a HomePod mini 2.

If you already own one original HomePod mini and want stereo sound, you'll need to find another first-generation model or purchase two newer speakers. You can't mix generations.

Sound Glow isn't exclusive to the new speaker

Sound Glow gives the HomePod mini 2's illuminated touch surface a more colorful appearance during music playback. The lighting draws colors from album artwork and pulses along with the music, adding a little movement to an otherwise understated design.

You won't need a new HomePod mini to enjoy the effect, though. Apple also brought Sound Glow to the original HomePod mini and second-generation HomePod through HomePod software 27.2.

The lighting is a welcome visual addition, especially if your speaker sits somewhere visible while you're listening. Since existing HomePods support the same feature, Sound Glow doesn't provide much incentive to upgrade.

Siri AI remains the biggest missing feature

Siri AI could eventually become one of the HomePod mini 2's biggest improvements, but the upgraded assistant still isn't available on the speaker as of November 4, 2026.

Apple has promised more natural conversations, broader knowledge, and better music discovery, along with requests that use personal information from supported apps. Users will eventually be able to ask Siri to find a song mentioned in a message or create a reminder using information stored elsewhere on their devices.

The expanded capabilities could make Siri more useful for everyday requests, especially when a command involves information spread across different apps. For now, HomePod mini 2 owners are still working with the existing assistant, and Apple hasn't announced a specific release date for the upgrade.

Getting the new Siri features will also involve more than updating the speaker. The home owner will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running compatible software, with Siri AI enabled.

Requests involving personal context will require a paired compatible device, although other household members will be able to use some conversational and knowledge features without owning one themselves.

Siri AI has the potential to make the HomePod mini 2 more appealing, particularly for households that rely heavily on voice commands. Until Apple releases the update, though, we can't judge how accurately the assistant responds or how much its new abilities improve daily use.

We'll be re-reviewing the HomePod Mini 2 when it launches.

Four-speaker surround sound comes at a price

The HomePod mini 2 also supports a new four-speaker surround sound arrangement when paired with the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K. The system uses matching front and rear speaker pairs, automatically adjusting audio timing and levels based on their positions in the room.

You can build the setup using four HomePod mini 2 speakers or combine two minis with two second-generation full-sized HomePods. The arrangement offers another option for Apple TV owners who want something more immersive than a traditional stereo pair.

We couldn't test the four-speaker surround sound setup because we don't have a new Apple TV 4K yet. We'll take a closer look at surround sound pairing and its performance in our upcoming Apple TV 4K review.

Building a setup from scratch also requires a considerable investment. Four HomePod mini 2 speakers cost $596, and the new Apple TV 4K is priced at $299, bringing the minimum total to $895 before tax.

For someone who already owns compatible HomePods, the new arrangement could be worth exploring when the required Apple TV arrives. Anyone buying all the hardware specifically for surround sound should compare the complete system with other home theater options before spending nearly $900.

Smart home features remain familiar

The HomePod mini 2 continues to serve as an Apple Home hub, giving users a way to control compatible accessories and run automations. Thread networking and built-in temperature and humidity sensors also remain available for smart home setups.

Anyone upgrading from the original HomePod mini will already have access to those features. Apple's first-generation speaker supports the same basic smart home capabilities, so the newer model doesn't fundamentally change what you can control.

For someone starting an Apple Home setup, the HomePod mini 2 still offers a useful combination of smart speaker and home hub. Existing owners can continue using their original HomePods for most of the same tasks.

HomePod mini 2 is better for new buyers than existing owners

The HomePod mini 2 delivers good sound with excellent room coverage and enough volume for everyday listening. Our lossless comparison revealed slightly better instrument separation than the original, giving the newer speaker a modest but noticeable audio advantage.

Apple has also expanded what the speaker can do beyond playing music. Persistent Mac audio and four-speaker surround sound could make the HomePod mini 2 more useful in different parts of the home, although neither feature has been fully evaluated in our testing.

Siri AI remains another potentially significant improvement, but you shouldn't base the purchase on an assistant update that hasn't arrived.

At $149, we'd recommend the HomePod mini 2 more readily to someone buying their first HomePod or expanding an existing setup than to someone replacing a working original.

If you already own a HomePod mini and primarily use it for music, Siri commands, and Apple Home, you'll get slightly better sound and newer hardware by upgrading. The improvements are welcome, but they aren't substantial enough to justify replacing speakers that already do their jobs well.

HomePod mini 2 pros

  • Clear, balanced sound
  • Better instrument separation with lossless music
  • Excellent room coverage
  • Updated wireless connectivity and expanded audio options
  • Useful Apple Home hub functionality

HomePod mini 2 cons

  • Modest audio improvements over the original HomePod mini
  • Siri AI isn't available at launch
  • Can't create a stereo pair with the original HomePod mini
  • Four-speaker surround requires expensive additional hardware

Score: 3 out of 5

The HomePod mini 2 is a product in the midst of becoming more. Siri AI may change it enough to justify a higher score, and surround sound pairing on Apple TV hardware may too.

We'll see. Like I said before, we'll re-review when Siri AI works on the model.

For now, if you have an original HomePod mini, stick with that. There's not enough justification to pay more for functionality you have right now.

Where to buy the HomePod mini 2

Apple's HomePod mini 2 retails for $149 and can be ordered at B&H Photo, Expercom, and Adorama.

items.title: Apple's bond sale is now confirmed at $7.5 billion
items.content_html:
Details of Apple's expected bond sale have now been confirmed in SEC filings, which show the company aims to raise a slightly higher than expected $7.5 billion.

It had been reported that Apple was aiming to raise around $7 billion through this bond offering, which is the sale of debt. That report was based on a preliminary filing with the SEC, but now the final pricing term sheet has been published.

This filing confirms that Apple plans to issue bonds in seven series that would mature between 2028 and 2036:

  • 2028: $500 million in floating-rate bonds plus $1 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 4.65% annual interest rate
  • 2029: $750 million in floating-rate bonds plus $1 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 4.75% annual interest rate
  • 2031: $1 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 4.90% annual interest rate
  • 2033: $1.25 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 5.10% annual interest rate
  • 2036: $2 billion in fixed-rate bonds with a 5.35% annual interest rate

Those floating-rate bonds will be at interest rates tied to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), which is adjusted every quarter. The fixed-rate notes are obviously constant.

What Apple gets

While the filing is for $7.5 billion, Apple actually expects to get around $7.47 billion. That's accounting for various costs and discounts.

Apple has filed that it intends the proceeds to be spent on "general corporate purposes, including repurchases of our common stock and payment of dividends under our program to return capital to shareholders, funding for working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions and repayment of debt."

There is no breakdown of what proportion of the $7.47 billion will be spent on any of these areas.
